claim: During maturation, DC cortical stiffness increases via a process that involves actin polymerization.
source: Using atomic force microscopy, we find that during maturation, DC cortical stiffness increases via a process that involves actin polymerization.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by AFM measurements and drug inhibition studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: Increasing stiffness lowers the agonist dose needed for T cell activation.
source: Using stimulatory hydrogels and DCs expressing mutant cytoskeletal proteins, we find that increasing stiffness lowers the agonist dose needed for T cell activation.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by hydrogel experiments showing dose-response curves shift with stiffness.

claim: CD4+ T cells exhibit much more profound stiffness dependency than CD8+ T cells.
source: CD4+ T cells exhibit much more profound stiffness dependency than CD8+ T cells.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this, supported by comparative experiments shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: Stiffness responses are most robust when T cells are stimulated with pMHC rather than anti-CD3ε.
source: Finally, stiffness responses are most robust when T cells are stimulated with pMHC rather than anti-CD3ε, consistent with a mechanosensing mechanism involving receptor deformation.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by comparative experiments in Figure 6.

claim: Maturation-associated cytoskeletal changes alter the biophysical properties of DCs, providing mechanical cues that costimulate T cell activation.
source: Taken together, our data reveal that maturation-associated cytoskeletal changes alter the biophysical properties of DCs, providing mechanical cues that costimulate T cell activation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, synthesizing multiple experimental findings.

claim: T cell activation by dendritic cells involves forces exerted by the T cell actin cytoskeleton, which are opposed by the cortical cytoskeleton of the interacting antigen-presenting cell.
source: T cell activation by dendritic cells (DCs) involves forces exerted by the T cell actin cytoskeleton, which are opposed by the cortical cytoskeleton of the interacting antigen-presenting cell.
evidence: This statement in the abstract draws on established knowledge about T cell-APC interactions.

claim: During an immune response, DCs undergo a maturation process that optimizes their ability to efficiently prime naïve T cells.
source: During an immune response, DCs undergo a maturation process that optimizes their ability to efficiently prime naïve T cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DC biology stated in the abstract.

claim: The initiation of an adaptive immune response requires priming of naïve T cells by professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs).
source: The initiation of an adaptive immune response requires priming of naïve T cells by professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs).
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge stated in the introduction.

claim: APCs transmit signals through multiple receptor-ligand interactions at the immunological synapse.
source: This process involves multiple receptor-ligand interactions, which occur in concert at a specialized cell-cell contact site called the immunological synapse (Dustin, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dustin, 2014.

claim: Following initial T cell receptor (TCR) engagement, T cells apply cycles of pushing and pulling forces on interacting APCs.
source: Following initial T cell receptor (TCR) engagement, T cells apply cycles of pushing and pulling forces on interacting APCs (Bashour et al., 2014; Blumenthal and Burkhardt, 2020; Hui et al., 2015; Husson et al., 2011; Sawicka et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Forces applied by T cells are essential for proper T cell activation.
source: These forces are essential for proper T cell activation (Li et al., 2010; Pryshchep et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Li et al., 2010 and Pryshchep et al., 2014.

claim: Force application is responsible, at least in part, for the ability of T cells to rapidly discriminate between agonist and antagonist antigens.
source: Moreover, force application is responsible, at least in part, for the ability of T cells to rapidly discriminate between agonist and antagonist antigens (Das et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Das et al., 2015 and Liu et al., 2014.

claim: Early tyrosine phosphorylation events downstream of TCR engagement occur at sites where applied force is maximal.
source: Interestingly, the amount of force a T cell applies is directly affected by the stiffness of the stimulatory substrate (Husson et al., 2011; Sawicka et al., 2017). Thus, it appears that force application is mechanically coupled to the T cell's ability to sense stiffness (mechanosensing). In other cell types, substrate stiffness has been shown to affect a variety of cell functions including differentiation, migration, growth, and survival (Byfield et al., 2009; Discher et al., 2005; Engler et al., 2006; Lo et al., 2000; Oakes et al., 2009; Pelham and Wang, 1997; Solon et al., 2007; Trappmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bashour et al., 2014.

claim: The amount of force a T cell applies is directly affected by the stiffness of the stimulatory substrate.
source: Interestingly, the amount of force a T cell applies is directly affected by the stiffness of the stimulatory substrate (Husson et al., 2011; Sawicka et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Husson et al., 2011 and Sawicka et al., 2017.

claim: Substrate stiffness affects both initial priming and effector functions of T cells.
source: Stiffness sensing in T cells has not been well studied, though there is some evidence that substrate stiffness affects both initial priming and effector functions (Alatoom et al., 2020; Basu et al., 2016; Judokusumo et al., 2012; O'Connor et al., 2012; Saitakis et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Dendritic cells (DCs) are the dominant APCs that prime T cells in vivo.
source: Dendritic cells (DCs) are the dominant APCs that prime T cells in vivo (Jung et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jung et al., 2002.

claim: Immature DCs are sentinels of the immune system, specialized for immune surveillance and antigen processing.
source: Immature DCs are sentinels of the immune system, specialized for immune surveillance and antigen processing (Mellman and Steinman, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mellman and Steinman, 2001.

claim: Inflammatory stimuli trigger signaling pathways that induce molecular reprogramming of DCs during maturation.
source: In response to infection or injury, inflammatory stimuli trigger signaling pathways that induce molecular reprogramming of the cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DC maturation.

claim: Mature DCs express high levels of surface ligands and cytokines needed for efficient T cell priming.
source: The resulting mature DCs express high levels of surface ligands and cytokines needed for efficient T cell priming (Burns et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Burns et al., 2004.

claim: Remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton is a central feature of DC maturation.
source: A central feature of DC maturation is remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton, a process that underlies other maturation-associated changes such as downregulation of endocytosis and increased migratory behavior (Garrett et al., 2000; West et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Garrett et al., 2000 and West et al., 2000.

claim: Cytoskeletal remodeling has a direct impact on the ability of mature DCs to prime T cells.
source: Cytoskeletal remodeling also has a direct impact on the ability of mature DCs to prime T cells (Al-Alwan et al., 2001; Comrie et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Al-Alwan et al., 2001 and Comrie et al., 2015.

claim: Depolymerization of actin filaments perturbs the ability of mature peptide-pulsed DCs to activate T cells.
source: Indeed, depolymerization of actin filaments perturbs the ability of mature peptide-pulsed DCs to activate T cells, indicating that actin plays an important role on the DC side of the immunological synapse.
evidence: This statement draws on established findings about the role of actin in DC function.

claim: Immature BMDCs have a mean Young's modulus of 2.2 ± 1.7 kPa.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, immature BMDCs were quite soft, with a mean Young's modulus of 2.2 ± 1.7 kPa.
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mature BMDCs have a Young's modulus of 3.3 ± 1.4 kPa.
source: Mature BMDCs were almost 2-fold stiffer, with a Young's modulus of 3.3 ± 1.4 kPa.
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The stiffness of CD86-negative BMDCs within the LPS-treated population is 2.0 ± 1.0 kPa, the same as that of untreated, immature DCs.
source: Importantly, the stiffness of CD86-negative BMDCs within the LPS-treated population was 2.0 ± 1.0, the same as that of untreated, immature DCs.
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The observed increase in stiffness is a property of DC maturation rather than an unrelated response to lipopolysaccharide treatment.
source: This demonstrates that the observed increase in stiffness is a property of DC maturation rather than an unrelated response to lipopolysaccharide treatment.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that CD86-negative cells in LPS-treated populations have the same stiffness as untreated cells.

claim: The stiffness of immature splenic DCs is 1.9 ± 0.7 kPa.
source: Results were very similar; the stiffness of immature splenic DCs was 1.9 ± 0.7, and lipopolysaccharide treatment induced a 2.5-fold increase in stiffness resulting in mature splenic DCs with a mean Young's modulus of 4.8 ± 1.7 kPa (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Lipopolysaccharide treatment induces a 2.5-fold increase in stiffness of splenic DCs.
source: Results were very similar; the stiffness of immature splenic DCs was 1.9 ± 0.7, and lipopolysaccharide treatment induced a 2.5-fold increase in stiffness resulting in mature splenic DCs with a mean Young's modulus of 4.8 ± 1.7 kPa (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct measurement and calculation reported in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mature splenic DCs have a mean Young's modulus of 4.8 ± 1.7 kPa.
source: Results were very similar; the stiffness of immature splenic DCs was 1.9 ± 0.7, and lipopolysaccharide treatment induced a 2.5-fold increase in stiffness resulting in mature splenic DCs with a mean Young's modulus of 4.8 ± 1.7 kPa (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Stiffness modulation is a bona fide trait of DC maturation.
source: These results demonstrate that stiffness modulation is a bona fide trait of DC maturation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from measurements of both BMDCs and splenic DCs.

claim: The biologically relevant range of DC stiffness lies between 2 and 8 kPa.
source: Moreover, they establish that the biologically relevant range of DC stiffness lies between 2 and 8 kPa.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the measured stiffness values of immature and mature DCs.

claim: Neither cytochalasin-D nor latrunculin-B affects the stiffness of immature BMDCs.
source: Neither drug affected the stiffness of immature BMDCs, indicating that the basal level of stiffness depends on factors other than the actin cytoskeleton (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The basal level of stiffness in immature DCs depends on factors other than the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Neither drug affected the stiffness of immature BMDCs, indicating that the basal level of stiffness depends on factors other than the actin cytoskeleton (Figure 1C).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that actin depolymerizing drugs do not affect immature DC stiffness.

claim: Both cytochalasin-D and latrunculin-B induce a significant decrease in the stiffness of mature DCs.
source: By contrast, both drugs induced a significant decrease in the stiffness of mature DCs, with cytochalasin reducing their stiffness to that of immature DCs.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cytochalasin reduces the stiffness of mature DCs to that of immature DCs.
source: By contrast, both drugs induced a significant decrease in the stiffness of mature DCs, with cytochalasin reducing their stiffness to that of immature DCs.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The increased cortical stiffness observed upon DC maturation is a feature of actin cytoskeletal reprogramming.
source: We conclude that the increased cortical stiffness observed upon DC maturation is another feature of actin cytoskeletal reprogramming.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the drug inhibition experiments showing actin-dependence of mature DC stiffness.

claim: Substrate compliance does not affect cortical stiffness of either immature or mature BMDCs.
source: As shown in Figure 1D, substrate compliance did not affect cortical stiffness of either immature or mature BMDCs.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: DCs maintain a specific cortical stiffness, which is characteristic of their maturation state.
source: Thus, we conclude that DCs maintain a specific cortical stiffness, which is characteristic of their maturation state.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that substrate stiffness does not affect DC cortical stiffness.

claim: The stiffness of BMDCs from fascin-/- mice is not significantly different from that of WT BMDCs either before or after LPS-induced maturation.
source: Surprisingly, the stiffness of BMDCs from fascin-/- mice was not significantly different from that of WT BMDCs either before or after LPS-induced maturation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Treating mature BMDCs with the myosin II inhibitor blebbistatin reduces stiffness by a small, albeit statistically significant amount.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, treating mature BMDCs with the myosin II inhibitor blebbistatin reduced stiffness by a small, albeit statistically significant amount.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Rho-kinase (ROCK) inhibitor Y27623 reduces the stiffness of mature BMDCs.
source: Similar results were obtained with the Rho-kinase (ROCK) inhibitor Y27623, which indirectly inhibits myosin function.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Treatment of DCs with the pan-formin inhibitor SMIFH2 significantly reduces the cortical stiffness of mature DCs.
source: Treatment of DCs with the pan-formin inhibitor SMIFH2 significantly reduced the cortical stiffness of mature DCs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Inhibition of Arp2/3-mediated branched actin polymerization by CK666 produces the most profound reduction in mature DC stiffness.
source: The most profound reduction was observed after inhibition of Arp2/3-mediated branched actin polymerization by CK666.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The loss of HS1 has no impact on cortical stiffness of either immature or mature BMDCs.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, the loss of HS1 had no impact on cortical stiffness of either immature or mature BMDCs.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mature WASp knockout BMDCs are significantly less stiff than WT controls.
source: By contrast, mature WASp knockout BMDCs were significantly less stiff than WT controls.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The stiffness difference in WASp knockout DCs mirrors that seen after inhibition of Arp2/3 complex by CK666.
source: This difference mirrors that seen after inhibition of Arp2/3 complex by CK666, suggesting that WASp is the primary activator of Arp2/3 complex-dependent changes in cortical stiffness.
evidence: This is a comparison drawn from the experimental data.

claim: WASp is the primary activator of Arp2/3 complex-dependent changes in cortical stiffness.
source: This difference mirrors that seen after inhibition of Arp2/3 complex by CK666, suggesting that WASp is the primary activator of Arp2/3 complex-dependent changes in cortical stiffness.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the similarity between WASp knockout and CK666 inhibition effects.

claim: The defect in WASp knockout DCs is observed only after maturation.
source: The defect in WASp knockout DCs was observed only after maturation; immature WASp knockout DCs did not differ in stiffness from WT controls.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Immature WASp knockout DCs do not differ in stiffness from WT controls.
source: The defect in WASp knockout DCs was observed only after maturation; immature WASp knockout DCs did not differ in stiffness from WT controls.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Activation of the WASp-dependent actin polymerization pathway contributes to the increased cortical stiffness of mature DCs.
source: Taken together, these results show that activation of the WASp-dependent actin polymerization pathway, and to a lesser extent increased myosin contractility and formin-mediated actin polymerization, all contribute to the increased cortical stiffness of mature DCs.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined results of drug inhibition and knockout experiments.

claim: Increased myosin contractility contributes to the increased cortical stiffness of mature DCs.
source: Taken together, these results show that activation of the WASp-dependent actin polymerization pathway, and to a lesser extent increased myosin contractility and formin-mediated actin polymerization, all contribute to the increased cortical stiffness of mature DCs.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined results of drug inhibition experiments.

claim: Formin-mediated actin polymerization contributes to the increased cortical stiffness of mature DCs.
source: Taken together, these results show that activation of the WASp-dependent actin polymerization pathway, and to a lesser extent increased myosin contractility and formin-mediated actin polymerization, all contribute to the increased cortical stiffness of mature DCs.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined results of drug inhibition experiments.

claim: CD4+ T cells show profound stiffness-dependent response at 24 hr across all measures of activation.
source: As shown in Figure 3A–C, CD4+ T cells showed a profound stiffness-dependent response at 24 hr across all measures.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Increasing substrate stiffness enhances the CD4+ T cell response in a graded manner for upregulation of CD25 and CD69.
source: This response was most clearly seen for upregulation of CD25 and CD69, where increasing substrate stiffness enhanced the CD4+ T cell response in a graded manner.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Increasing substrate stiffness lowers the pMHC-II dose required to obtain the same level of CD4+ T cell activation.
source: However, comparison among stimulatory surfaces revealed that increasing substrate stiffness lowered the pMHC-II dose required to obtain the same level of activation.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Over the stiffness range associated with DC maturation (2–8 kPa), the dose of TCR signal needed to induce surface marker upregulation in CD4+ T cells is shifted by 1–2 logs.
source: Over the stiffness range associated with DC maturation (2–8 kPa), the dose of TCR signal needed to induce surface marker upregulation was shifted by 1–2 logs.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation drawn from the dose-response curves in Figure 3A-B.

claim: IL-2 production by CD4+ T cells increases almost 3-fold when stimulated on surfaces of 8 kPa, as opposed to 2 kPa, for the same antigen dose.
source: IL-2 production increased almost 3-fold when CD4+ T cells were stimulated on surfaces of 8 kPa, as opposed to 2 kPa, for the same antigen dose.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CD8+ T cells show little to no stiffness sensitivity for upregulation of surface activation markers.
source: Strikingly, the robust stiffness response we observed in CD4+ T cells was not recapitulated for CD8+ T cells, especially when T cell activation was assessed based on surface marker upregulation (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: Analysis of IL-2 production reveals stiffness-enhanced activation of naïve CD8+ T cells.
source: Analysis of IL-2 production did reveal stiffness-enhanced activation of naïve CD8+ T cells; as in CD4+ T cells, this was clearest across the stiffness range associated with DC maturation.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Increasing substrate stiffness produces graded increases in CD4+ T cell proliferation.
source: Similar to what was observed for early activation markers, increasing substrate stiffness produced graded increases in CD4+ T cell proliferation, and the threshold dose required to induce robust proliferation shifted as a function of substrate stiffness (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The threshold dose required to induce robust CD4+ T cell proliferation shifts as a function of substrate stiffness.
source: Similar to what was observed for early activation markers, increasing substrate stiffness produced graded increases in CD4+ T cell proliferation, and the threshold dose required to induce robust proliferation shifted as a function of substrate stiffness (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The stiffness effect on CD4+ T cell proliferation is particularly evident at low doses of pMHC-II (0.1–1 ug/mL).
source: This effect was particularly evident at low doses of pMHC-II (0.1–1 ug/mL).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Soft hydrogels (2–4 kPa) induce upregulation of CD25 in a high percentage of CD4+ T cells, even in the undivided populations.
source: Interestingly, although soft hydrogels (2–4 kPa) elicited only very low levels of CD4+ T cell proliferation, these substrates did induce upregulation of CD25 in a high percentage of CD4+ T cells, even in the undivided populations (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: An activating signal is received on soft substrates, but is insufficient to drive CD4+ T cell proliferation.
source: This indicates that an activating signal was received, but was insufficient to drive proliferation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that CD25 is upregulated without proliferation on soft substrates.

claim: Addition of exogenous IL-2 does not rescue the proliferation of CD4+ T cells stimulated on soft surfaces.
source: Interestingly, addition of IL-2 did not rescue the proliferation of T cells stimulated on soft surfaces, nor did it increase proliferation on stiffer ones (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Substrate stiffness affects IL-2 independent events needed for efficient T cell proliferation.
source: Thus, we conclude that in addition to influencing the signaling threshold for IL-2 production, substrate stiffness also affects other IL-2 independent events needed for efficient T cell proliferation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that exogenous IL-2 does not rescue proliferation on soft substrates.

claim: CD8+ T cells show mild stiffness-dependent proliferation.
source: Although early activation events in CD8+ T cells showed little to no stiffness sensitivity, CD8+ T cells showed mild stiffness-dependent proliferation (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: The concentration of stimulatory ligand needed to induce at least one round of CD8+ T cell division is similar across the entire stiffness range.
source: The concentration of stimulatory ligand needed to induce at least one round of division was similar across the entire stiffness range Over successive rounds, increased stiffness did enhance the extent of proliferation, but the differences were relatively small (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CD8+ T cells exhibit a binary stiffness response at low doses of peptide ligand.
source: Interestingly, analysis of CFSE dilution as a function of CD25 expression reveals evidence that CD8+ T cells exhibit a binary stiffness response (Figure 5C,D); at low doses of peptide ligand, cells stimulated on very stiff substrates (25 kPa or plastic) survived and proliferated, whereas cells stimulated on softer substrates were mostly lost (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: At low doses of peptide ligand, CD8+ T cells stimulated on very stiff substrates (25 kPa or plastic) survived and proliferated, whereas cells stimulated on softer substrates were mostly lost.
source: Interestingly, analysis of CFSE dilution as a function of CD25 expression reveals evidence that CD8+ T cells exhibit a binary stiffness response (Figure 5C,D); at low doses of peptide ligand, cells stimulated on very stiff substrates (25 kPa or plastic) survived and proliferated, whereas cells stimulated on softer substrates were mostly lost (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The more robust stiffness response of CD4+ vs CD8+ T cells stems from differences in the cells themselves, rather than the properties of the particular pMHC/TCR pairs used for investigation.
source: Thus, we conclude that the more robust stiffness response of CD4+ vs CD8+ T cells stems from differences in the cells themselves, rather than the properties of the particular pMHC/TCR pairs used for investigation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experiments using anti-CD3 stimulation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Stiffer substrates have a sensitizing effect on CD4+ T cells, similar to that of classical costimulatory molecules such as CD28.
source: Taken together, our findings point to a mechanism in which stiffer substrates have a sensitizing effect on CD4+ T cells, similar to that of classical costimulatory molecules such as CD28 (Harding et al., 1992).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, supported by a citation.

claim: The relative lack of stiffness responses in CD8+ T cells fits with the fact that CD8+ T cells are much less dependent on costimulatory signals.
source: When considered in this way, the relative lack of stiffness responses in CD8+ T cells fits with the fact that CD8+ T cells are much less dependent on costimulatory signals (McAdam et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, supported by a citation.

claim: Degranulation of effector OTI CTLs shows only a mild stiffness dependency.
source: Degranulation showed only a mild stiffness dependency (Figure 5E), and stiffness tended to affect the magnitude of degranulation rather than whether or not a degranulation response was triggered.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Changes in substrate stiffness within the range defined for DCs (2–8 kPa) have little or no impact on CTL degranulation.
source: Interestingly, changes in substrate stiffness within the range of defined for DCs (2–8 kPa) had little or no impact on degranulation.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Increased degranulation of CTLs is only seen on stiffer surfaces (12 and 25 kPa).
source: Increased degranulation was only seen on stiffer surfaces (12 and 25 kPa).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: All three ligands (anti-CD3ε, anti-TCRβ, and pMHC-II) induce a stiffness-dependent response for both proliferation and CD25 expression in CD4+ T cells.
source: All three ligands induced a stiffness-dependent response for both proliferation and CD25 expression, but the responses differed in significant ways.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Stimulating CD4+ T cells with pMHC-II results in the strongest responses on hydrogel surfaces.
source: In general, stimulating T cells with pMHC-II resulted in the strongest responses on the hydrogel surfaces; only on plastic surfaces did anti-CD3ε stimulation yield a similarly strong response (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 6A,C.

claim: On surfaces with a stiffness similar to that of mature DCs (8 kPa), stimulation with pMHC results in robust CD4+ T cell proliferation, while stimulation with anti-CD3ε yields a minimal response.
source: Importantly, on surfaces with a stiffness similar to that of mature DCs (8 kPa), stimulation with pMHC resulted in robust proliferation, while stimulation with anti-CD3ε yielded a minimal response.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 6.

claim: On soft substrates (2–4 kPa), pMHC elicits some CD4+ T cell proliferation, whereas stimulation with anti-CD3 does not.
source: On softer substrates (2–4 kPa), pMHC elicited some proliferation, whereas stimulation with anti-CD3 did not.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 6.

claim: At high doses of antigen, stimulation with anti-TCRβ results in clear proliferative responses on substrates within the biologically-relevant stiffness range.
source: Interestingly, stimulation with anti-TCRβ resulted in a mixed response. At high doses of antigen, stimulation with anti-TCRβ yielded clear proliferative responses on substrates within the biologically-relevant stiffness range.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 6.

claim: On soft surfaces, pMHC yields the strongest CD25 expression response, and anti-TCRβ is more effective than anti-CD3ε.
source: Analysis of CD25 expression patterns revealed a similar trend (Figure 6D–F); on soft surfaces, pMHC yielded the strongest response, and anti-TCRβ was more effective than anti-CD3ε.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: T cells sense substrate stiffness best through direct engagement of TCRαβ.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that T cells sense substrate stiffness best through direct engagement of TCRαβ as predicted by the receptor deformation model.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparison of different stimulation methods shown in Figure 6.

claim: Mature WASp-KO BMDCs are approximately 20% softer than WT controls.
source: We took advantage of our finding that mature WASp-KO BMDCs are approximately 20% softer than WT controls (Figure 2A; data are presented as absolute values in Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: WASp-KO BMDCs do not prime T cells as efficiently as WT BMDCs at low OVA concentrations.
source: As shown in Figure 7B, WASp-KO BMDCs did not prime T cells as efficiently as WT BMDCs at low OVA concentrations.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Higher concentrations of OVA rescue the T cell priming defect of WASp-KO BMDCs.
source: Higher concentrations of OVA rescued this defect, showing that loss of WASp shifts the dose of peptide needed rather than affecting T cell priming per se, in keeping with the view that DC stiffness provides a costimulatory signal.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Loss of WASp shifts the dose of peptide needed for T cell priming rather than affecting T cell priming per se.
source: Higher concentrations of OVA rescued this defect, showing that loss of WASp shifts the dose of peptide needed rather than affecting T cell priming per se, in keeping with the view that DC stiffness provides a costimulatory signal.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the dose-response experiments with WASp-KO BMDCs.

claim: Overexpression of a constitutively active form of WASp (I294T, CA-WASp) increases cortical stiffness of mature BMDCs by approximately 20% relative to WT cells.
source: We did find that overexpression of a constitutively active form of WASp (I294T, CA-WASp [Beel et al., 2009]) increased cortical stiffness of mature BMDCs by approximately 20% relative to WT cells (Figure 7A), but these BMDCs failed to prime T cells more efficiently (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: BMDCs overexpressing CA-WASp fail to prime T cells more efficiently than WT BMDCs.
source: We did find that overexpression of a constitutively active form of WASp (I294T, CA-WASp [Beel et al., 2009]) increased cortical stiffness of mature BMDCs by approximately 20% relative to WT cells (Figure 7A), but these BMDCs failed to prime T cells more efficiently (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Changes in DC stiffness impact their ability to efficiently prime a T cell response.
source: Nonetheless, the studies using WASp-KO DCs show that changes in DC stiffness impact their ability to efficiently prime a T cell response.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the WASp-KO DC priming experiments.

claim: Actin remodeling during DC maturation increases the cortical stiffness of DC by 2–3-fold.
source: We show that actin remodeling during DC maturation increases the cortical stiffness of DC by 2–3-fold, and that T cell activation is enhanced by increases in stiffness over the same range.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the AFM and T cell activation experiments.

claim: Increased stiffness lowers the threshold dose of TCR ligand needed for T cell activation.
source: Importantly, increased stiffness lowers the threshold dose of TCR ligand needed for T cell activation, as expected if substrate stiffness serves as a costimulatory signal.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the hydrogel experiments.

claim: CD4+ T cells show more profound stiffness-sensitivity than CD8+ T cells, especially at early times in the activation process.
source: In keeping with this concept, CD4+ T cells showed more profound stiffness-sensitivity than CD8+ T cells, especially at early times in the activation process.
evidence: This is a summary of the comparative findings between CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.

claim: Stiffening of the DC cortex during maturation provides biophysical cues that work together with canonical costimulatory cues to enhance T cell priming.
source: Together, these results indicate that stiffening of the DC cortex during maturation provides biophysical cues that work together with canonical costimulatory cues to enhance T cell priming.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, synthesizing all experimental findings.

claim: Immature DCs are very soft.
source: We show that immature DCs are very soft, and that upon maturation, their cortical stiffness is increased by 2–3-fold.
evidence: This is a summary of the AFM measurements.

claim: Bufi et al., 2015 reported a similar trend for human monocyte-derived DCs, although that study reported lower absolute Young's modulus values.
source: A similar trend was reported by Bufi et al., 2015 for human monocyte-derived DCs, although that study reported lower absolute Young's modulus values.
evidence: This is a comparison with published literature.

claim: Different methods for measuring cell mechanical properties produce absolute Young's modulus values that can vary by as much as 100-fold.
source: Since different methods for measuring cell mechanical properties produce absolute Young's modulus values that can vary by as much as 100-fold (Wu et al., 2018), it seems likely that the apparent discrepancy in absolute values stems from technical differences between the two studies.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2018.

claim: Mature DCs exhibit characteristic membrane veils, as well as microvilli-rich regions that serve as preferred docking sites for T cells.
source: In particular, mature DCs exhibit characteristic membrane veils, as well as microvilli-rich regions that serve as preferred docking sites for T cells (Fisher et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fisher et al., 2008.

claim: DC maturation is known to induce changes in the activation state and localization of Rho family GTPases, especially Cdc42.
source: In keeping with these findings, DC maturation is known to induce changes in the activation state and localization of Rho family GTPases, especially Cdc42, a molecule that can activate both WASp and formins (Garrett et al., 2000; Vargas et al., 2016; West et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Garrett et al., 2000; Vargas et al., 2016; West et al., 2000.

claim: The overall levels of active Cdc42 are diminished during DC activation.
source: Since the overall levels of active Cdc42 are diminished during DC activation, it seems likely that the observed increase in cortical stiffness results from redistribution of the active pool.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about DC maturation.

claim: The observed increase in cortical stiffness likely results from redistribution of the active Cdc42 pool.
source: Since the overall levels of active Cdc42 are diminished during DC activation, it seems likely that the observed increase in cortical stiffness results from redistribution of the active pool.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on known changes in Cdc42 during DC maturation.

claim: DC cortical stiffness is a cell-intrinsic property that is unaffected by substrate stiffness.
source: We show that DC cortical stiffness is a cell-intrinsic property that is unaffected by substrate stiffness.
evidence: This is a summary of the substrate compliance experiments.

claim: DCs rapidly change their method of locomotion to maintain consistent migration speed and shape while crossing over different surfaces.
source: The ability of DCs to maintain constant stiffness despite changing environmental cues is reminiscent of previous work showing that DCs rapidly change their method of locomotion to maintain consistent migration speed and shape while crossing over different surfaces (Renkawitz et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Renkawitz et al., 2009.

claim: The ability of DCs to regulate cortical stiffness as a function of maturation state in spite of environmental cues reflects the importance of this property for priming an appropriate T cell response.
source: In the same way, we propose that the ability of DCs to regulate cortical stiffness as a function of maturation state in spite of environmental cues reflects the importance of this property for priming an appropriate T cell response.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Changes in DC stiffness serve as a costimulatory signal for T cell priming.
source: A central finding of this study is that changes in DC stiffness serves as a costimulatory signal for T cell priming.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Increases in cortical stiffness, together with diminished ligand mobility, represent biophysical cues that are modulated in parallel with upregulation of costimulatory ligands and cytokines as a fundamental part of DC maturation.
source: Our results indicate that increases in cortical stiffness, together with diminished ligand mobility (Comrie et al., 2015), represent biophysical cues that are modulated in parallel with upregulation of costimulatory ligands and cytokines as a fundamental part of DC maturation.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the current findings with previous work, supported by a citation.

claim: Treatment with the tolerizing cytokines TNFα and prostaglandin E2 results in DCs that are even softer than immature cells.
source: Bufi et al., 2015 showed previously that human monocyte-derived DCs responding to different maturation signals vary in their stiffness. Interestingly, they found that treatment with the tolerizing cytokines TNFα and prostaglandin E2 results in DCs that are even softer than immature cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bufi et al., 2015.

claim: Tolerogenic DCs exhibiting partially immature phenotypes induce differentiation of regulatory T cells.
source: Tolerogenic DCs exhibiting partially immature phenotypes have been shown to induce differentiation of regulatory T cells (Doan et al., 2009; Gleisner et al., 2011; Gordon et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Doan et al., 2009; Gleisner et al., 2011; Gordon et al., 2014.

claim: Biophysical properties of the DC cortex play a role in inducing differentiation of regulatory T cells.
source: This effect is usually attributed to low expression of T cell ligands or cytokines, but based on our data, we propose that biophysical properties of the DC cortex also play a role.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Re-stimulation of human CD4+ effector T cells on soft surfaces induces upregulation of genes related to cytokine signaling and proliferation.
source: Similarly, recent analysis of human CD4+ effector T cells shows that re-stimulation on soft surfaces induces upregulation of genes related to cytokine signaling and proliferation, while restimulation on very stiff surfaces (100 kPa) triggers expression of an additional genetic program that includes metabolic proteins related to glycolysis and respiratory electron transport (Saitakis et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Saitakis et al., 2017.

claim: Re-stimulation of human CD4+ effector T cells on very stiff surfaces (100 kPa) triggers expression of metabolic proteins related to glycolysis and respiratory electron transport.
source: Similarly, recent analysis of human CD4+ effector T cells shows that re-stimulation on soft surfaces induces upregulation of genes related to cytokine signaling and proliferation, while restimulation on very stiff surfaces (100 kPa) triggers expression of an additional genetic program that includes metabolic proteins related to glycolysis and respiratory electron transport (Saitakis et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Saitakis et al., 2017.

claim: T cells exert force on an interacting APC through the TCR complex.
source: The observation that T cells respond to APC stiffness is best understood in the context of evidence that T cells exert force on an interacting APC through the TCR complex (Bashour et al., 2014; Blumenthal and Burkhardt, 2020; Hui et al., 2015; Husson et al., 2011; Li et al., 2010; Sawicka et al., 2017), with the amount of force corresponding to APC stiffness (Husson et al., 2011; Sawicka et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The amount of force T cells exert corresponds to APC stiffness.
source: The observation that T cells respond to APC stiffness is best understood in the context of evidence that T cells exert force on an interacting APC through the TCR complex (Bashour et al., 2014; Blumenthal and Burkhardt, 2020; Hui et al., 2015; Husson et al., 2011; Li et al., 2010; Sawicka et al., 2017), with the amount of force corresponding to APC stiffness (Husson et al., 2011; Sawicka et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Husson et al., 2011 and Sawicka et al., 2017.

claim: Force transduction promotes peptide discrimination by influencing bond lifetimes.
source: Apart from being a requirement for activation (Li et al., 2010; Pryshchep et al., 2014), force transduction has been shown to promote peptide discrimination by influencing bond lifetimes (Das et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Das et al., 2015 and Liu et al., 2014.

claim: Signaling downstream of TCR engagement is increased on stiffer substrates.
source: Indeed, there is evidence that signaling downstream of TCR engagement is increased on stiffer substrates (Alatoom et al., 2020; Judokusumo et al., 2012) and that the intracellular location of early tyrosine phosphorylation events corresponds to sites of maximum traction force (Bashour et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Alatoom et al., 2020; Judokusumo et al., 2012; and Bashour et al., 2014.

claim: Stiffer substrates allow T cells to exert more force through TCR interactions, and consequently induce more effective signaling.
source: We propose that stiffer substrates allow T cells to exert more force through TCR interactions, and consequently induce more effective signaling.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Force applied on the TCR complex induces conformational changes within TCRαβ that expose ITAM sites on the CD3 and TCRζ chains for phosphorylation and downstream signaling.
source: Nevertheless, there is evidence to suggest that force applied on the TCR complex induces conformational changes within TCRαβ that exposes ITAM sites on the CD3 and TCRζ chains for phosphorylation and downstream signaling (Lee et al., 2015; Swamy et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2015 and Swamy et al., 2016.

claim: Conformational changes in the TCR are mainly attributed to the extension of the CβFG loop region within TCRβ.
source: Importantly, conformational changes are mainly attributed to the extension of the CβFG loop region within TCRβ (Das et al., 2015), which serves as a lever to push down on the CD3 complex (Sun et al., 2001), exposing ITAM sites (Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Das et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2001; and Xu et al., 2008.

claim: Direct TCRαβ engagement leads to conformational changes that are transmitted appropriately for efficient initiation of downstream signaling.
source: We postulate that direct TCRαβ engagement leads to conformational changes that are transmitted appropriately for efficient initiation of downstream signaling, whereas engagement of CD3 induces smaller changes and more limited downstream signaling.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Engagement of CD3 induces smaller conformational changes and more limited downstream signaling compared to direct TCRαβ engagement.
source: We postulate that direct TCRαβ engagement leads to conformational changes that are transmitted appropriately for efficient initiation of downstream signaling, whereas engagement of CD3 induces smaller changes and more limited downstream signaling.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: pMHC induces stronger T cell activation than anti-TCRβ on soft substrates, which may reflect the involvement of CD4.
source: We note that on these soft substrates, pMHC induced stronger T cell activation than anti-TCRβ. This may reflect the involvement of CD4 in the former, which leads to more efficient recruitment of Lck to the TCR complex.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the observed difference.

claim: pMHC complexes show relatively high lateral mobility in the DC membrane, even after maturation.
source: One caveat to our work is that pMHC complexes are immobilized on the hydrogel surfaces used here, whereas pMHC complexes show relatively high lateral mobility in the DC membrane, even after maturation (Comrie et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Comrie et al., 2015.

claim: Stiffness-dependent cytokine production by CTLs has been reported.
source: Similarly, Saitakis et al. have shown that restimulating CD4+ effector T cells on surfaces of different stiffness induces differential gene expression and cytokine production (Saitakis et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tello-Lafoz et al., 2020.

claim: Restimulating CD4+ effector T cells on surfaces of different stiffness induces differential gene expression and cytokine production.
source: Similarly, Saitakis et al. have shown that restimulating CD4+ effector T cells on surfaces of different stiffness induces differential gene expression and cytokine production (Saitakis et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Saitakis et al., 2017.

claim: Mechanosensing may be an obligate component of the feedback loop that underlies force-dependent TCR triggering.
source: It is possible that mechanosensing is not needed for effector function per se, but that it is an obligate component of the feedback loop that underlies force-dependent TCR triggering.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The mechanical properties of the APC side of the IS influence T cell priming because they augment force-dependent conformational changes in TCRs, integrins, and potentially other molecules.
source: Together with our recent work on ligand mobility, the findings presented here indicate that the mechanical properties of the APC side of the IS influence T cell priming, likely because they augment force-dependent conformational changes in TCRs, integrins, and potentially other molecules.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the current findings with previous work.
